stem: Which bone is the longest and strongest in the human body?
explanation: The femur is the major bone of the thigh and is described as the longest and strongest bone. The tibia bears weight in the leg, while the fibula is more slender and the humerus belongs to the upper limb.

stem: Which feature belongs to the proximal end of the femur?
explanation: The proximal femur contains the head, neck and greater and lesser trochanters. The patellar surface is distal; the tibial plateau and medial malleolus belong to the tibia.

stem: Which proximal tibial surface articulates with the femoral condyles?
explanation: The tibial plateau receives the femoral condyles at the knee. The tuberosity provides ligament attachment rather than the main femorotibial articular surface.

stem: The patellar ligament attaches distally to which landmark?
explanation: The roughened tibial tuberosity is the distal attachment of the patellar ligament. This links the patella to the tibia as part of the knee extensor mechanism.

stem: Which of these is a tarsal bone?
explanation: The navicular is one of the tarsals in the foot. Scaphoid, capitate and lunate are carpal bones in the wrist.

stem: Which vessels connect superficial and deep venous systems of the lower limb?
explanation: Lower-limb venous drainage includes superficial, deep and perforating veins. Perforating veins provide connections between the superficial and deep systems; the other options are not lower-limb connecting veins.

stem: Which ligaments convert the sciatic notches into foramina?
explanation: The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments complete the boundaries of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. These openings transmit structures between the pelvis and adjacent regions.

stem: Which is a principal action of gluteus maximus?
explanation: Gluteus maximus extends and laterally rotates the thigh at the hip. Toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion involve leg muscles rather than gluteus maximus.

stem: Which muscle belongs to the deep gluteal group?
explanation: Piriformis is listed among the small deep gluteal muscles. Rectus femoris and sartorius are anterior thigh muscles; gracilis is in the medial compartment.

stem: The superior and inferior gluteal arteries arise from which artery?
explanation: The major gluteal arterial branches arise from the internal iliac artery. Their pelvic origin explains their passage through the greater sciatic foramen to reach the gluteal region.

stem: The hip is classified as which type of joint?
explanation: The spherical femoral head articulates with the acetabulum, allowing multiaxial movement. This arrangement defines a ball-and-socket synovial joint.

stem: Which structure deepens the acetabular socket?
explanation: The acetabular labrum is a rim that increases socket depth and helps retain the femoral head. The other structures do not form the acetabular rim.

stem: Which bone is a sesamoid within the quadriceps tendon?
explanation: The patella develops within the quadriceps tendon and articulates with the anterior distal femur. Its position is characteristic of a sesamoid bone.

stem: Which bone fits into the ankle mortise?
explanation: The trochlea of the talus fits into the mortise formed by the distal tibia and fibula. The calcaneus lies below the talus and is not the bone received by the mortise.

stem: In which position is the ankle mortise grip on the talus strongest?
explanation: Dorsiflexion brings the wider anterior trochlea into the mortise and tightens the malleolar grip. Plantarflexion brings the narrower portion into the mortise and is relatively less stable.

stem: Which nerve primarily supplies the anterior thigh compartment?
explanation: The anterior thigh compartment includes quadriceps and is primarily supplied by the femoral nerve. The obturator nerve mainly supplies medial thigh adductors.

stem: Which nerve primarily supplies the medial thigh compartment?
explanation: The medial compartment contains the adductors and is primarily supplied by the obturator nerve. Part of adductor magnus has additional sciatic innervation, so “primarily” is important.

stem: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle?
explanation: Sartorius forms the lateral boundary, adductor longus the medial boundary and the inguinal ligament the superior boundary of the femoral triangle.

stem: Where is the popliteal fossa located?
explanation: The popliteal fossa is the diamond-shaped depression posterior to the knee. It transmits important nerves and vessels between the thigh and leg.

stem: Which pair forms the hindfoot?
explanation: The hindfoot contains the talus and calcaneus. Navicular, cuboid and the cuneiforms form the midfoot; metatarsals form part of the forefoot.

stem: Which ligament helps support the medial longitudinal arch?
explanation: The spring ligament helps support the medial longitudinal arch together with tibialis posterior and the plantar aponeurosis. The other named ligaments are not supports of this arch.

stem: Which substance in radiographic film is responsible for photosensitivity?
explanation: The emulsion contains photosensitive silver-halide crystals. Polyester supports the film and lead foil reduces backscatter in dental packets; neither is the photosensitive constituent.

stem: Which film arrangement is typically used for high-detail film-screen mammography?
explanation: Single-emulsion film is selected where fine detail is important and is used in mammography film-screen systems. The lecture contrasts this with double-emulsion film used commonly in general screen-film radiography.

stem: What is the main function of the radiographic film base?
options: Conversion of X-rays into visible light
explanation: The polyester base supports the emulsion and provides strength and rigidity. Image formation occurs in the emulsion, while intensifying screens convert X-rays to light.

stem: Why is a modern polyester film base commonly tinted blue?
explanation: The blue tint improves viewing comfort on a viewbox. It is not the photosensitive element and cannot replace chemical processing.

stem: Which film layer forms the image?
explanation: The emulsion holds silver-halide crystals in gelatin and is the image-forming layer. The base and adhesive provide support and attachment.

stem: What is the role of gelatin in the emulsion?
options: Holds crystals and permits chemical penetration
explanation: Gelatin distributes and holds the silver-halide crystals while allowing developer and fixer to reach them. Blocking processing chemicals would prevent development.

stem: Which silver halide is commonly the main constituent of radiographic film crystals?
explanation: Silver bromide is the main halide described, sometimes with smaller quantities of iodide or chloride. These crystals undergo the exposure changes that create the latent image.

stem: What is the latent image?
explanation: The latent image is the invisible change in exposed silver-halide crystals. Development converts those changes into visible black metallic silver.

stem: What is the main purpose of an intensifying screen?
explanation: An intensifying screen absorbs X-rays and emits light that exposes compatible film efficiently. Fixing and drying are separate processing functions.

stem: A technician observes blur from poor screen-film contact. What should be checked?
explanation: Poor contact allows emitted screen light to spread before reaching the film, reducing sharpness. Cassette condition and contact therefore form part of quality assurance.

stem: Which layer bonds the emulsion to the film base?
explanation: The adhesive, substratum or subbing layer prevents the emulsion from lifting off the base during handling and processing. The supercoat protects the outer surface.

stem: What is the principal function of the supercoat?
explanation: The thin hard gelatin supercoat protects the emulsion from mechanical damage. It is distinct from the photosensitive emulsion and from processing chemicals.

stem: What is the purpose of lead foil backing in intraoral dental film packets?
explanation: Lead foil backing reduces radiation backscatter that could reach the film and degrade the image. The packet must also remain light-tight and protected from moisture.

stem: Developer primarily converts exposed silver-halide crystals into what?
explanation: Developer reduces exposed crystals to metallic silver, creating the visible image. Fixer instead removes unexposed silver halide.

stem: What happens if washing after fixing is inadequate?
options: Residual chemicals may cause later staining
The base becomes a digital detector
The film becomes immune to light
explanation: Residual fixer and related compounds impair archival stability and may cause discoloration. Washing removes these processing residues before drying and filing.

stem: How should unprocessed radiographic film be handled?
options: By gripping the emulsion with wet hands
By dragging it over rough surfaces
By the edges with clean dry hands
explanation: Edge handling reduces fingerprints, pressure marks and scratches. Wet or contaminated fingers can produce chemical artefacts before the film even enters processing.

stem: Which stock-control method best reduces expired film use?
explanation: Using the earliest-expiring stock first reduces age-related waste and fog. Batch numbers and expiry dates should remain traceable.

stem: A film shows black branching tree-like marks. What is the likely cause?
explanation: Static discharge produces branching black marks, particularly with dry air and rapid film removal. Gentle handling and humidity control reduce this artefact.

stem: Why should film spectral sensitivity match the intensifying screen?
options: To prevent any need for fixing
For efficient response to emitted light
To eliminate all need for radiation
explanation: Film must respond to the screen’s emitted wavelengths to form the image efficiently. A mismatch wastes useful light and may lead to unnecessary exposure.

stem: Green-sensitive film is also called what?
explanation: Orthochromatic radiographic film is sensitive to green light and pairs with compatible green-emitting rare-earth screens. Safelight selection must follow the film specification.

stem: Which adjustment changes the displayed tissue range on a CT hard copy?
explanation: Window settings select the grey-scale display of CT attenuation values, allowing different presentations for lung, bone or soft tissue. Physical film handling cannot perform that numerical display adjustment.

stem: Which computer component temporarily holds active programs and data?
explanation: Random-access memory holds data in current use. An SSD provides longer-term storage; printers are output devices and barcode scanners are input devices.

stem: Which component processes data and controls computer operations?
explanation: The central processing unit executes instructions and coordinates operations. The other devices provide input, output or storage.

stem: Which is an input device used in radiography?
explanation: A barcode scanner enters identification data into a system. Monitors, printers and speakers deliver output to a user.

stem: Which device provides persistent image storage?
explanation: An SSD retains stored data when power is off, unlike ordinary RAM. Secure backups are still needed because persistent storage can fail.

stem: Which imaging system reconstructs cross-sectional images from multiple X-ray projections?
explanation: CT computer systems reconstruct tomographic images from multiple X-ray projections. PACS stores images, RIS manages workflow and word processors handle documents.

stem: What is the main role of PACS?
options: Store retrieve and distribute medical images
explanation: PACS supports image archiving, retrieval, display and distribution. It is an information system rather than an X-ray production or chemical-processing device.

stem: Which system primarily manages appointments worklists and radiology reports?
explanation: A Radiology Information System handles departmental workflow, patient registration, examination scheduling and reporting. PACS focuses on images rather than these administrative workflows.

stem: What does DICOM provide?
options: A standard for medical image exchange
explanation: Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine standardizes medical image formatting and exchange. It is a communication standard, not a physical detector or chemical.

stem: Which is an example of raw technical data?
explanation: A recorded kVp value is a raw technical fact. A diagnostic report is processed and interpreted information that supports clinical decisions.

stem: What best describes information?
explanation: Information has been processed or interpreted to provide meaning. Raw readings and unorganized facts are data before that transformation.

stem: A report reaches the clinician after the decision is already made. Which quality is most directly lacking?
explanation: Information must be available when needed to support decisions. Accuracy and completeness matter too, but the particular problem here is late delivery.

stem: Which application is most suitable for preparing a departmental referral letter?
explanation: Word processors create, edit and format text documents such as letters and reports. Detector tools and exposure meters serve different technical functions.

stem: Which feature produces personalized letters from a template and data source?
explanation: Mail merge combines a document template with records to create individualized documents. Image windowing and laser scanning do not perform document personalization.

stem: Which application best supports calculations and departmental statistics?
explanation: Spreadsheet software organizes numeric data and supports calculations and statistical summaries. Word processors and presentation tools are better suited to prose and slides.

stem: Medical X-ray CT and MRI images are commonly exchanged in which format?
explanation: DICOM can retain image data and associated medical information in a standardized form. Audio files and executables are not standard medical image exchange formats.

stem: What is the purpose of file backup?
options: Guarantee no access control is needed
explanation: A backup protects against loss or damage to the primary file. It must itself be secured and does not replace access controls.

stem: Which practice best protects transmitted patient images?
explanation: Approved encrypted channels and authorized access protect confidentiality. Public sharing and shared credentials expose identifiable clinical data.

stem: What should a technician verify before transmitting images?
explanation: Correct identifiers help ensure images are associated with the intended patient and recipient workflow. Transmission speed does not compensate for a patient-identification error.

stem: What is a clinical risk of excessive digital image processing?
options: All source data become more accurate
explanation: Overprocessing may introduce misleading appearances or hide detail. Processing changes image presentation and cannot undo radiation already delivered.

stem: What is a major benefit of teleradiology?
explanation: Digital communication allows images to reach specialists at other locations. It still requires secure systems, correct identifiers and appropriate professional roles.

stem: What makes daylight film handling possible?
options: Removing all silver halide before exposure
explanation: The enclosure shields sensitive film from ambient light during handling. Daylight processing never means that unprocessed film can be left uncovered in ordinary room light.

stem: What occurs after the cassette is placed into a daylight loading compartment?
options: Protected cassette opening and film extraction
Removal of the X-ray tube anode
Conversion of the room into a laser scanner
Immediate public display of unprocessed film
explanation: The cassette opens inside a protected compartment and the exposed film is extracted safely. It then passes through chemical-processing stages.

stem: Which component prevents ambient-light fogging in a daylight processor?
explanation: The light-tight chamber prevents room light from reaching sensitive film. The collection tray receives finished film but is not the main protection during loading.

stem: Which limitation remains with daylight film processing?
options: Film is insensitive to all light
explanation: Daylight systems improve handling convenience but still rely on chemical processing and mechanical equipment. Chemical replenishment and maintenance remain necessary.

stem: How does a daylight loader differ from a film processor?
options: Loader protects and transfers film; processor performs chemical processing
Loader alone converts X-rays to digital pixels
Both are always the same device
explanation: The lecture distinguishes light-protected film transfer from chemical development, fixing, washing and drying. Some installations integrate both functions, but they remain distinct tasks.

stem: Which receptor is used in computed radiography?
explanation: CR stores a latent image in a photostimulable phosphor plate and requires reader scanning. Direct flat-panel detectors are a different receptor system.

stem: What is the function of an ADC?
options: Convert analog signals to numerical values
explanation: An analog-to-digital converter samples and quantizes an electrical signal into digital numerical values. It does not perform shielding or chemical processing.

stem: How does a CR plate store a latent image?
options: Energy trapped in phosphor electron states
explanation: X-ray energy traps electrons in metastable states within the phosphor. Laser stimulation later releases stored energy as light for readout.

stem: What releases stored image energy during CR readout?
explanation: The CR reader scans the plate with a laser, stimulating emission of light from trapped energy. That emitted light is then detected and converted to an electrical signal.

stem: Why is a CR plate exposed to intense light after readout?
explanation: Erasure removes residual stored energy and prepares the plate for reuse. Incomplete erasure can leave residual-image artefacts.

stem: What physical principle underlies CR plate readout?
explanation: CR phosphor releases stored energy as light when stimulated by a laser. This is photostimulable luminescence and differs from film chemical development.

stem: Which CR plate layer stores X-ray exposure energy?
explanation: The phosphor layer holds the latent image. Protective and support layers provide mechanical protection but do not perform the principal storage function.

stem: Which material is associated with direct-conversion DR?
explanation: Amorphous selenium converts X-ray energy directly into electrical charge. Indirect detectors first convert X-rays into light through a scintillator.

stem: Which material can act as a scintillator in indirect DR?
explanation: Cesium iodide converts X-rays into visible light. Photodiodes then convert this light into charge; thiosulfate and acetic acid belong to film-processing chemistry.

stem: What converts scintillator light to charge in indirect DR?
explanation: The photodiode converts light into electrical charge. The scintillator performs the preceding X-ray-to-light conversion.

stem: What is the role of the TFT array?
options: Switch and read out pixel charge
explanation: Thin-film transistors act as switches that allow pixel signals to be read by detector electronics. They are part of detector readout rather than X-ray production.

stem: Which workflow difference distinguishes CR from most DR systems?
options: CR requires a separate plate reader
explanation: CR stores a plate image that must be scanned in a reader. Most DR systems read electronic detector signals directly, improving image availability.

stem: Why can acceptable digital brightness conceal excessive exposure?
options: Patient dose is erased by windowing
Image brightness directly measures patient dose
explanation: Digital processing can maintain acceptable brightness over a wide exposure range. Exposure indicators and technique monitoring are therefore needed to reduce dose creep.

stem: Which operation adjusts displayed contrast and brightness?
explanation: Windowing and leveling remap digital image values for display. They change presentation and do not alter the exposure that has already occurred.

stem: Can processing reliably recover anatomy that was never captured?
options: No; acquisition must contain the information
explanation: Postprocessing can improve presentation of acquired data. It cannot reliably recreate anatomy outside the captured field or information absent from the original acquisition.

stem: Does switching to digital imaging automatically reduce patient dose?
options: No; exposure technique still requires optimisation
Yes because detectors emit no light
explanation: Digital imaging offers dose-optimisation opportunities but does not guarantee lower exposure. Technique, detector performance and radiation-protection practice remain essential.

stem: Which electrode receives accelerated electrons in an X-ray tube?
explanation: The positive anode receives electrons emitted from the negative cathode. Their interaction with the target generates heat and X-rays.

stem: What is the function of the cathode assembly?
explanation: The cathode provides electron emission from the heated filament and helps focus electrons toward the target. The anode receives those electrons.

stem: Why is filtration placed in the X-ray beam?
options: Convert film into a digital image
Remove low-energy photons with little imaging benefit
explanation: Low-energy photons may be absorbed in the patient without contributing useful detector information. Filtration reduces that low-energy component; collimation separately limits field size.

stem: What is the primary purpose of high tube voltage?
explanation: A large potential difference provides electrons with kinetic energy as they cross the evacuated tube. Filament heating uses a different low-voltage high-current circuit.

stem: What does an exposure timer control?
explanation: The timer terminates X-ray production after the selected exposure interval. Timing affects delivered exposure and must be reproducible.

stem: Which is a function of the X-ray generator?
options: Control tube voltage current and exposure time
explanation: The generator supplies and controls electrical conditions for X-ray production. Patient records and film-processing chemistry are separate systems.

stem: Which device restricts the X-ray field to the area of interest?
explanation: Collimators limit the exposed area and reduce unnecessary irradiation and scatter production. They act before radiation enters the patient.

stem: Which is a beam-centering device?
explanation: A light-beam localizer indicates the beam field and assists alignment with the anatomical area. It does not chemically process or store film.

stem: What is the safety role of an anode rotation interlock?
options: Increase exposure regardless of tube readiness
Prevent exposure when rotation is inadequate
explanation: An interlock prevents unsafe exposure when required operating conditions are not met. Inadequate anode rotation may concentrate heat and damage the target.

stem: What is the principal function of a fuse?
explanation: A fuse breaks the circuit when current exceeds its safe capacity. It protects electrical equipment rather than directly changing detector image contrast.

stem: What initiates electron emission in a conventional X-ray tube?
options: Cooling the anode to zero kelvin
explanation: Heating the tungsten filament releases electrons by thermionic emission. High voltage then accelerates these electrons toward the target.

stem: Bremsstrahlung results primarily from what?
options: Laser erasure of a CR plate
Electron deceleration near a target nucleus
explanation: The incoming electron loses kinetic energy as it is deflected and decelerated in the nuclear electric field. The lost energy is emitted as an X-ray photon, producing a continuous spectrum.

stem: What event leads to characteristic radiation?
options: A grid moves across the detector
An outer electron fills an inner-shell vacancy
A laser erases residual plate energy
Film is exposed to a safelight
explanation: An incident electron ejects an inner-shell electron. When another electron fills that vacancy, the energy difference is emitted as a characteristic photon.

stem: What is a main effect of scatter reaching the receptor?
options: Conversion of X-rays to magnetic fields
explanation: Scatter adds unwanted exposure that is not correctly related to the primary anatomical path. This degrades contrast and may add noise.

stem: Where is an anti-scatter grid placed?
options: Between the filament and focusing cup
explanation: A grid intercepts scatter emerging from the patient before it reaches the image receptor while allowing appropriately aligned primary radiation through.

stem: How is grid ratio defined?
options: Source distance divided by patient age
Exposure time divided by tube current
Lead strip height divided by interspace width
Film width divided by film length
explanation: Grid ratio compares lead-strip height with the distance between strips. It describes grid geometry and influences scatter rejection and alignment demands.

stem: Why is a grid moved during exposure in a Bucky assembly?
options: Change the atomic number of lead
explanation: Grid movement spreads strip shadows over the exposure so distinct grid lines are less visible. It does not immobilize the patient or produce tube electrons.

stem: What is an important trade-off when using an anti-scatter grid?
options: Exposure factors and patient dose may increase
explanation: A grid absorbs some primary radiation as well as scatter. Exposure compensation may therefore be needed, increasing patient dose; grid use should be justified for the examination.

stem: Which modality provides real-time moving X-ray images?
explanation: Fluoroscopy produces real-time images of internal movement. Film storage and densitometry do not perform real-time patient imaging.

stem: Which equipment is commonly used for intraoperative real-time imaging?
explanation: The mobile C-arm positions an X-ray source and receptor around the operative field for procedural imaging. The other devices serve processing or administrative functions.

stem: Which mechanism advances film through an automatic processor?
explanation: Roller racks and crossover components guide film through solutions and the dryer at controlled speed. This mechanical consistency helps standardize processing time.

stem: Which subsystem helps keep chemical baths homogeneous?
explanation: Recirculation mixes solutions, limits temperature gradients and filters particles. These actions support consistent chemical processing across the film surface.

stem: What is the purpose of automatic replenishment?
options: Maintain chemical activity and solution levels
Remove the need for quality control
explanation: Processing consumes and dilutes chemistry, while oxidation also reduces activity. Replenishment introduces fresh chemicals to stabilize performance, but does not replace QA.

stem: How should films be fed to reduce roller jams?
options: With wet fingers on the emulsion
explanation: Straight, spaced feeding reduces overlap and transport misalignment. Bent or overlapping films can jam and damage the emulsion.

stem: What is the purpose of standby mode?
explanation: Standby reduces activity when no film is being processed and resumes operation when film is detected. It is an efficiency function, not permission to bypass processing conditions.

stem: Which variables are standardized in automatic processing?
options: Only wall color and room size
explanation: Automatic systems control transport time, bath temperature and chemistry to achieve reproducible processing. Each variable affects image density and contrast.

stem: Why is developer temperature controlled precisely?
explanation: Developer reaction rate changes with temperature. Poor regulation can alter density, contrast and fog, so the actual temperature should be verified.

stem: Which sequence describes the automatic processor path?
options: Wash then dryer then fixer then developer
Fixer then developer then dryer then wash
Developer then fixer then wash then dryer
Dryer then wash then developer then fixer
explanation: Automatic film processing develops the image, fixes it, removes chemical residues by washing and then dries it. Reordering these stages would not form a stable diagnostic film.

stem: What commonly detects film entry at the feed tray?
explanation: Entry sensors detect film and trigger transport, drying and replenishment functions. A dosimeter measures exposure rather than film entry.

stem: Which feed arrangement permits handling under normal room light?
explanation: The enclosed daylight loader prevents room light from reaching sensitive film. An ordinary uncovered tray still requires a darkroom and appropriate safelight conditions.

stem: Which rollers first grip film just beyond the feed tray?
explanation: Entrance rollers engage film at the start of transport. Deep-tank rollers guide it through chemistry and squeegee rollers remove excess water later.

stem: What is the principal role of crossover rollers?
options: Guide film between adjacent processing tanks
explanation: Crossover assemblies redirect film from one rack or tank to the next. Dirty or misaligned parts can cause marks and scratches.

stem: What do squeegee rollers do before drying?
options: Add more fixer to the emulsion
explanation: Squeegee rollers press excess water from the film and reduce the drying load. This helps the dryer produce a dry finished film efficiently.

stem: Volume replenishment is commonly triggered according to what?
explanation: Entry sensors estimate film dimensions or processed area and the system delivers a specified replenisher volume. This relates replenishment to workload.

stem: Why is timed flood replenishment useful in low-volume departments?
options: Combat oxidation despite low film throughput
Prevent every form of patient motion
explanation: Chemistry can oxidize even when few films are processed. Timed replenishment introduces fresh chemistry at intervals independent of film throughput.

stem: Why should standard manual chemistry not simply be used in an automatic processor?
options: Rollers remove all need for hardeners
Automatic chemistry must tolerate high speed and temperature
explanation: Rapid processing at elevated temperatures requires specially formulated chemistry, including control of emulsion swelling. The manufacturer’s specified chemistry should be followed.

stem: Which agent acts as a developer hardener in automatic processing?
explanation: Glutaraldehyde limits gelatin swelling under automatic-processing conditions. Cesium iodide is a scintillator and barium sulfate is a contrast material.

stem: Why is a cleaner film passed before patient films during startup?
explanation: A cleaner film lifts dried chemistry and debris from the transport pathway. This reduces contamination and artefacts on subsequent patient films.

stem: A film shows repeating roller-related marks. What should be inspected?
explanation: Contamination or damage on a rotating roller can produce recurring marks. Cleaning or replacing the affected component addresses the cause; mark spacing depends on roller geometry.

stem: Which instrument measures control-film optical density?
explanation: A densitometer measures optical density at control-film steps. These values help track base plus fog, speed and contrast as part of processor quality assurance.

stem: What is a monobath?
options: One solution providing development and fixation
explanation: A monobath combines developing and fixing actions in one balanced solution. Washing and drying remain necessary after this combined chemical stage.

stem: Which chemical provides the fixing action in a monobath?
explanation: Thiosulfate acts as a silver-halide solvent, dissolving unexposed crystals. The developer and fixer actions must be balanced in a monobath.

stem: What is an important limitation of monobath processing?
options: Limited control of contrast and image quality
explanation: Combining two chemical functions reduces independent control and the solution can exhaust rapidly. The lecture therefore does not recommend it for routine diagnostic work.

stem: What distinguishes conventional manual processing?
options: All chemistry in one unlabelled tank
Separate developer rinse fixer and wash stages
explanation: Separate baths allow each chemical stage to be controlled and maintained independently. A monobath instead combines development and fixation.

stem: What is the usual chemical character of developer?
explanation: The developer is alkaline, which supports the reducing agents. Fixer is acidic and removes unexposed silver halide.

stem: According to the lecture what is a typical manual development condition?
explanation: The lecture gives approximately five minutes at 20°C as a reference manual condition. Actual time-temperature combinations should follow the film and chemical manufacturer’s chart.

stem: Why should film move through tanks in one direction?
explanation: A one-way workflow prevents film and drips from contaminating stages it has already left. Separate lids and stirring rods also help preserve solution purity.

stem: What is the function of the master tank water jacket?
explanation: Water surrounding the inner tanks exchanges heat through the walls and helps maintain a common stable temperature. It is not itself a substitute for developer or fixer.

stem: Which darkroom layout principle reduces film contamination?
options: Mix wet chemicals on the loading bench
Keep unexposed film beside open fixer
explanation: A dry zone supports clean film loading while a wet zone contains chemical processing. Separation reduces water, chemical and handling artefacts.

stem: What is the primary use of the darkroom dry bench?
explanation: The dry bench provides a clean area for handling sensitive film and cassettes. Wet chemical work belongs at the wet bench.

stem: What is a film hopper used for?
explanation: A hopper stores unexposed film ready for loading while protecting it from light. It is part of the dry-side storage system.

stem: Which material is suitable for a processing tank?
explanation: The lecture recommends stainless steel 316 or polypropylene for chemical resistance. Copper, brass and galvanized metals can corrode or contaminate processing chemistry.

stem: Why should processing tanks be covered when idle?
explanation: Covers reduce contact with air and keep out dust. This helps preserve chemistry and supports consistent image quality.

stem: Which developer ingredient acts as a restrainer to limit fog?
explanation: Potassium bromide restrains development of unexposed crystals and limits fog. Thiosulfate clears film in fixer, acetic acid acidifies and alum hardens gelatin.

stem: What is the function of sulfite in developer?
explanation: Sulfite is a preservative that slows oxidation of developing agents. It helps maintain chemical activity during use and storage.

stem: Which fixer ingredient dissolves unexposed silver halide?
explanation: Thiosulfate is the clearing agent in fixer. Hydroquinone is a developing agent and carbonate provides alkalinity in developer.

stem: A film remains milky after fixation. What is a likely cause?
explanation: Insufficient removal of unexposed halide leaves a cloudy or milky appearance. Fixer strength and clearing time should be checked.

stem: A technician sees pale circular spots caused by bubbles during development. What is the prevention?
explanation: Air bells prevent developer from contacting parts of the emulsion and produce pale spots. Initial agitation and tapping dislodge these bubbles.

stem: Fixer splashed on film before development most likely causes what?
explanation: Fixer removes silver-halide material before it can develop, producing local light or white spots. Developer splashes can instead cause dark spots.

stem: What is the purpose of the rinse between developer and fixer?
options: Remove developer carryover and halt development
explanation: Rinsing removes alkaline developer from the emulsion and reduces contamination of the acidic fixer. It protects fixer life and helps reduce staining.

stem: The lecture recommends fixing for at least what relation to clearing time?
explanation: Clearing time indicates removal of visible cloudiness, while additional fixing supports more complete stabilization. The lecture gives at least twice clearing time, with manufacturer guidance controlling practice.

stem: What can cause brown staining during film storage?
explanation: Residual thiosulfate and silver compounds can cause later staining. Adequate running-water washing is necessary for archival stability.

stem: Which used solution is the main source of dissolved silver for recovery?
explanation: Fixer dissolves unexposed silver halide and accumulates silver compounds. It is therefore the main liquid source for silver recovery.

stem: Which silver recovery method deposits silver on a cathode?
explanation: Electrolytic recovery uses electrical current to deposit silver on a cathode. Metallic replacement instead uses a more reactive metal such as iron.

stem: Steel wool cartridges recover silver by which process?
explanation: Iron displaces silver from solution in a metallic-replacement process. This is a chemical recovery method rather than an imaging or readout mechanism.

stem: How should used fixer be managed?
options: Leave unlabelled in a patient area
Collect in labelled sealed containers for approved recovery or disposal
explanation: Used fixer contains silver and should be collected securely with disposal records. Recovery or approved waste handling prevents avoidable environmental contamination.

stem: What is the SI unit of radioactive activity?
explanation: The becquerel corresponds to one nuclear decay per second. Gray measures absorbed dose, sievert measures protection-weighted dose and volt measures potential difference.

stem: What does radioactive half-life describe?
options: Time for all radiation to cease
Time for half the radioactive atoms to decay
Time for every atom to gain an electron
explanation: Half-life is the time required for half of the initial radioactive nuclei to decay. It does not imply the entire sample becomes nonradioactive after one half-life.

stem: What is the SI unit of absorbed dose?
explanation: Absorbed dose measures energy deposited per unit mass. One gray is one joule per kilogram; activity and electrical quantities have different units.

stem: Equivalent and effective doses are expressed in which SI unit?
explanation: The sievert is used for protection quantities that incorporate radiation weighting, and for effective dose also tissue weighting. Absorbed dose itself is measured in gray.

stem: One gray corresponds to how many rad?
explanation: The lecture gives 1 Gy = 100 rad. These are different units of absorbed dose, not units of activity.

stem: One sievert corresponds to how many rem?
explanation: The sievert and rem measure equivalent or effective dose, with 1 Sv = 100 rem. They should not be confused with gray and rad for absorbed dose.

stem: What is the SI unit of force?
explanation: Force is measured in newtons. Joule measures energy or work, watt measures power and kelvin measures thermodynamic temperature.

stem: When a constant force acts along a displacement how is work calculated?
explanation: For force parallel to motion, work is W = Fd. The displacement must be in the force direction; the result is expressed in joules.

stem: What is the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature?
explanation: Kelvin is the SI base unit. Degrees Celsius are commonly used operationally, but are not the SI base unit.

stem: Heat is best described as what?
options: Energy transferred because of a temperature difference
explanation: Heat is energy in transit from higher to lower temperature. Temperature describes thermal state, while heat describes a transfer process.

stem: Which subatomic particle carries positive charge?
explanation: A proton has positive elementary charge. A neutron is electrically neutral, an electron is negative and an X-ray photon carries no electric charge.

stem: What determines the atomic number of an element?
explanation: Atomic number Z is the proton count and identifies the element. Protons plus neutrons determine mass number A.

stem: What is the maximum occupancy of the first electron shell?
explanation: The first shell holds up to two electrons. Higher shells have different capacities; shell occupancy should not be confused with atomic number.

stem: How is mass number defined?
explanation: The mass number counts nucleons: A = Z + N. Electrons contribute negligible mass relative to nucleons and are not included in mass number.

stem: Which electrons primarily govern chemical bonding?
explanation: Valence electrons occupy the outermost shell and govern bonding and chemical behavior. Nuclear composition instead defines the element and its isotopes.

stem: Isotopes of the same element differ in what?
explanation: Isotopes have the same proton number but different neutron counts, giving different mass numbers. A different proton count would define a different element.

stem: What is ionization?
options: An electron moving up a level while remaining bound only
A neutron becoming a detector pixel
Gain or loss of electrons producing net charge
A change in room temperature only
explanation: Ionization creates an ion by electron loss or gain. Excitation raises a bound electron to a higher energy state without necessarily removing it.

stem: What distinguishes excitation from ionization?
options: A proton always leaves the nucleus
The electron remains bound to the atom
explanation: Excitation places a bound electron at a higher energy level. Ionization involves electron removal or gain and a change in net charge.

stem: What is the SI unit of electric current?
explanation: Electric current is charge flow per unit time, measured in amperes. One ampere equals one coulomb per second.

stem: Potential difference is measured in which unit?
explanation: Voltage represents electrical energy per unit charge and is measured in volts. Current uses amperes and radiation quantities use different units.

stem: What is the SI unit of capacitance?
explanation: Capacitance expresses charge stored per unit potential difference and is measured in farads. Resistance is measured in ohms.

stem: Electromagnetic induction depends on which condition?
explanation: A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces electromotive force. Faster flux change or more coil turns increases induced voltage under Faraday’s law.

stem: What is the SI unit of resistance?
explanation: Resistance describes opposition to current flow and is measured in ohms. Voltage, current and charge have distinct SI units.

stem: A 12 V source is connected across 4 ohms. Calculate current.
explanation: Ohm’s law gives I = V/R. Substituting 12/4 gives 3 A; multiplying the values would give the wrong physical quantity.

stem: Which equation states Ohm’s law?
explanation: Voltage equals current multiplied by resistance for an ohmic conductor under the relevant physical conditions. Rearrangements are I = V/R and R = V/I.

stem: Three resistors of 100 20 and 30 ohms are in series. What is total resistance?
explanation: Series resistances add directly: 100 + 20 + 30 = 150 ohms. The same current flows through each resistor.

stem: Two 50-ohm resistors are in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?
explanation: For two parallel resistors, R = R1R2/(R1+R2). Thus 2500/100 = 25 ohms, less than either branch resistance.

stem: A 100-ohm resistor is in series with two parallel 50-ohm resistors. What is the total?
explanation: The parallel pair is 25 ohms. Adding the 100-ohm series resistor gives a total of 125 ohms.

stem: What is the SI unit of energy?
explanation: Energy is measured in joules. A watt is a joule per second and describes power rather than total energy.

stem: A lamp uses 60 joules every second. What is its power?
explanation: Power is energy transferred per unit time: P = E/t. Sixty joules per second is sixty watts.

stem: According to Joule’s heating law doubling current changes heat by what factor if resistance and time are constant?
explanation: H = I²Rt, so doubling current multiplies I² by four. Resistance and duration must be held constant for this comparison.

stem: How does a fuse interrupt an excessive current?
options: It stores all current as a magnetic image
explanation: Excess current produces Joule heating that melts the fuse element and opens the circuit. This prevents continued current flow through the protected circuit.

stem: Which energy source uses photovoltaic cells?
explanation: Photovoltaic cells convert light into electrical energy. Wind and hydropower instead drive turbines, while nuclear and fossil systems typically use thermal generation.

stem: What does electromotive force describe?
options: Energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue
Energy supplied per unit charge by a source
explanation: EMF describes energy a source supplies to each unit of charge and is measured in volts. Absorbed dose and activity are radiation quantities, not electrical EMF.

stem: How do X-ray photons behave in an electric field?
options: They are not deflected by charge forces
They bend toward the positive plate as electrons do
explanation: X-ray photons have no electric charge, so electric fields do not deflect them like charged particles. Their propagation and interactions differ from electron motion.

stem: What is the approximate speed of X-rays in vacuum?
explanation: X-rays are electromagnetic radiation and travel at the speed of light in vacuum. Their short wavelength does not make them travel faster than visible light in vacuum.

stem: Thermionic emission occurs at which component?
explanation: Heating the cathode filament releases electrons that form a space-charge cloud. High voltage then accelerates these electrons toward the anode.

stem: Approximately what fraction of electron energy becomes heat at a diagnostic X-ray target?
explanation: The lecture describes roughly 99% heat and about 1% X-ray production under typical diagnostic conditions. This low efficiency makes target heat management essential.

stem: What type of spectrum is produced by bremsstrahlung?
explanation: Different electron decelerations release different photon energies, creating a continuous spectrum. Characteristic radiation instead has discrete energies tied to atomic shell differences.

stem: Characteristic X-ray energy is determined by what?
options: Difference between atomic shell binding energies
explanation: An electron transition into an inner-shell vacancy releases the difference in binding energies as a photon. This yields energies characteristic of the target element.

stem: How many carpal bones are present in one hand?
explanation: The wrist has eight carpal bones in two rows. One hand also has five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges, which are separate bone groups.

stem: Which sequence describes the proximal carpal row from lateral to medial?
explanation: The proximal row is scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform. Trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate form the distal row.

stem: Which carpal belongs to the distal row?
explanation: Capitate is in the distal row with trapezium, trapezoid and hamate. The other options belong to the proximal row.

stem: Which muscle is an intrinsic shoulder muscle?
explanation: Deltoid is part of the intrinsic shoulder group together with teres major and rotator cuff muscles. The other listed muscles are extrinsic shoulder muscles.

stem: Which bones articulate at the glenohumeral joint?
explanation: The humeral head articulates with the glenoid cavity of the scapula. This is the ball-and-socket shoulder joint.

stem: Which structure deepens the glenoid cavity?
explanation: The fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum increases the depth of the shallow glenoid socket. This supports stability while allowing substantial shoulder movement.

stem: What is a major stabilizing muscle group at the shoulder?
explanation: The rotator cuff provides dynamic support to the shoulder joint. Quadriceps, hamstrings and triceps surae are lower-limb groups.

stem: Which muscle initiates shoulder abduction?
explanation: Supraspinatus initiates abduction, after which deltoid is the principal contributor. Latissimus dorsi and pectoralis major chiefly adduct, while subscapularis medially rotates.

stem: Which muscle is a principal shoulder extensor?
explanation: Latissimus dorsi is a chief extensor and is assisted by posterior deltoid fibres. The other muscles primarily position or stabilize the pectoral girdle.

stem: Which nerve supplies deltoid and is relevant in shoulder injury?
explanation: The axillary nerve is among the nerves related to the shoulder and supplies deltoid. Its anatomical relationship makes it important when assessing shoulder trauma.

stem: Where does pectoralis minor insert?
explanation: Pectoralis minor arises from upper ribs and inserts on the coracoid process of the scapula. The olecranon and radial styloid are distal upper-limb landmarks.

stem: What is a principal action of pectoralis major?
options: Adduction and medial rotation of the arm
explanation: Pectoralis major draws the arm toward the body and rotates it medially. Its action is at the shoulder, not the lower limb.

stem: Serratus anterior inserts mainly on which scapular surface?
options: Costal surface of the medial border
explanation: The muscle attaches to the costal aspect of the medial scapular border and helps position the scapula against the thoracic wall.

stem: Which nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the arm?
explanation: The anterior arm contains biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis and is supplied chiefly by the musculocutaneous nerve. The posterior compartment is supplied by the radial nerve.

stem: Which muscle is in the posterior arm compartment?
explanation: Triceps brachii is an elbow extensor in the posterior compartment, supplied by the radial nerve. The other options are anterior arm muscles.

stem: Which structure connects the shafts of radius and ulna?
explanation: The interosseous membrane joins the two forearm bones and helps transfer forces between them. The glenoid labrum belongs to the shoulder.

stem: The common flexor origin is at which humeral landmark?
explanation: The anterior forearm flexor-pronator group arises in part from the medial epicondyle. The common extensor origin is on the lateral epicondyle.

stem: Which muscle flexes the elbow despite lying in the forearm’s posterior compartment and receiving radial nerve supply?
explanation: Brachioradialis flexes the elbow but lies in the posterior compartment and has radial nerve supply. This is an exception to a simplistic flexor-versus-extensor innervation rule.

stem: Which nerve supplies the posterior forearm extensor group?
explanation: The posterior extensor-supinator group is supplied by the radial nerve and its branches. These muscles commonly arise from the lateral epicondyle.

stem: Compression of which nerve causes carpal tunnel syndrome?
explanation: The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. Compression can impair its sensory and motor functions; the other nerves do not traverse this tunnel.

stem: Which artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
explanation: The radial artery winds around the lateral wrist and crosses the snuffbox floor to reach the hand. This is an important surface-anatomy relationship.

stem: The thenar compartment is located at the base of which digit?
explanation: Thenar muscles form the thumb base. The hypothenar compartment is at the base of the little finger.

stem: The hypothenar compartment is associated with which digit?
explanation: Hypothenar muscles act on the little finger. The thumb has the distinct thenar muscle group.

stem: Why are hand fascial spaces clinically important?
options: They help localize infection and pus collections
explanation: Fascial septa define potential spaces that influence the spread and localization of infection. Knowledge of these spaces helps explain the pattern of hand infections.

stem: Teaching and specialist hospitals represent which level of health care?
explanation: The lecture groups clinics and health centres as primary, general hospitals as secondary and teaching or specialist hospitals as tertiary care.

stem: Which quality best supports good radiographic patient care?
explanation: Empathy supports the patient’s emotional needs, while accuracy and attention to detail protect technical quality and safety. Ignoring concerns undermines both care and communication.

stem: Which ethical principle respects a patient’s choices?
explanation: Autonomy recognizes the patient’s right to make informed choices. Beneficence concerns acting for good and non-maleficence concerns avoiding harm.

stem: Which principle means acting for the patient’s good?
explanation: Beneficence directs care toward the patient’s welfare. It complements autonomy, non-maleficence and justice rather than replacing them.

stem: Which ethical principle means do no harm?
explanation: Non-maleficence requires avoiding preventable harm, including unnecessary radiation exposure. Justice addresses fairness and confidentiality protects private information.

stem: Treating every patient fairly expresses which principle?
explanation: Justice concerns fairness in care and allocation of services. It is an ethical principle, not a technical image-production process.

stem: What should be confirmed before any patient exposure?
options: Only the time on the wall clock
explanation: Confirming identity helps prevent wrong-patient and wrong-examination errors. The request and intended examination must be matched to the patient before exposure.

stem: What is an appropriate approach to an anxious patient?
options: Make promises that discomfort is impossible
Explain each step and allow questions
explanation: Clear honest explanation and opportunities for questions reduce uncertainty. False reassurance and unexplained jargon can increase anxiety and undermine trust.

stem: Which is a patient right?
options: Loss of privacy during every procedure
explanation: Patients have rights to information, dignity, privacy and refusal. Respecting refusal requires appropriate communication and documentation within the clinical context.

stem: What is essential for informed consent?
options: Understanding the purpose benefits and risks
explanation: Consent depends on meaningful understanding and a voluntary choice. A signature alone does not demonstrate that the patient understood the procedure.

stem: Which behavior best preserves confidentiality?
options: Discuss identifiable cases in public corridors
Protect records and avoid public case discussions
explanation: Confidentiality requires secure handling and appropriate information sharing. Public discussion or unauthorized disclosure can damage trust and expose private patient information.

stem: Which history item is particularly relevant before contrast administration?
explanation: The lecture emphasizes allergies as part of patient history and checking relevant risks before contrast. History should be assessed with the responsible clinical team and protocol.

stem: What should be done with abnormal vital signs?
options: Ignore them if the image is needed
Assume they are always equipment errors
explanation: Vital signs reflect basic physiological function. Abnormal readings need timely reporting and appropriate clinical assessment rather than being ignored or removed.

stem: Which resting adult pulse range is given in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture gives 60–100 beats per minute as a normal adult reference range. Clinical interpretation still depends on the patient and circumstances.

stem: Which adult respiratory rate range is given in the lecture?
explanation: The reference adult respiratory range is 12–20 breaths per minute. Rate must be interpreted alongside clinical signs and the patient’s baseline.

stem: When hands are visibly soiled which hygiene method is appropriate?
options: Alcohol rub as the only method regardless of soiling
explanation: The lecture recommends washing with soap and water and allows alcohol rub when hands are not visibly soiled. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

stem: What is the basis of standard precautions?
options: Treat every patient as potentially infectious
Use precautions only for known infections
explanation: Standard precautions apply to all patients because infection status may be unknown. They include appropriate PPE, sharps safety and waste management.

stem: What should follow a needle-stick injury?
options: Immediate reporting and local exposure protocol
Recapping the needle and continuing silently
explanation: Prompt reporting allows assessment and timely post-exposure management according to local procedure. Concealment delays care and prevents proper incident review.

stem: Which measure is particularly appropriate for an elderly patient?
explanation: Older patients may have fragile skin, limited mobility or sensory impairment. Allowing extra time and preventing falls supports safe positioning and transfer.

stem: When transfer of a critically ill patient is unsafe what imaging approach may be appropriate?
options: Disconnect all monitors and transfer alone
explanation: The lecture supports mobile imaging when transfer is unsafe and coordination with nursing staff while maintaining airway, lines and monitoring.

stem: What does ALARA stand for?
explanation: ALARA is an optimisation principle: keep exposures as low as reasonably achievable while meeting the clinical imaging objective. It does not mean sacrificing necessary diagnostic information.

stem: Which three tools are emphasized for radiation protection?
explanation: Reducing exposure time, increasing distance and using appropriate shielding are core protective tools. Their use must fit the specific examination and working conditions.

stem: Which action helps avoid unnecessary repeat exposure?
options: Correct positioning and appropriate exposure selection
explanation: Accurate positioning and suitable technical factors improve the chance of a diagnostic first image. Avoidable repeats increase dose without adding intended benefit.

stem: What device monitors occupational radiation exposure?
explanation: A personal dosimeter tracks occupational exposure. A densitometer measures film optical density and a thermometer measures temperature.

stem: A patient collapses with airway swelling during contrast injection. What is the immediate response described?
options: Stop injection and call for emergency help
Continue injection to finish the dose
explanation: Collapse and airway swelling indicate a severe reaction requiring urgent assistance. Stop the injection, activate emergency response and follow the local emergency protocol and professional scope.

stem: What is health management in a radiology service?
options: Planning organization and coordination for safe efficient care
Only buying the most expensive machine
explanation: Management coordinates resources, people and workflow to support safe and efficient service. It includes more than equipment purchasing.

stem: Which activity is part of radiographic quality assurance?
explanation: Reject analysis identifies patterns of image failure and opportunities to reduce repeats. QA also includes equipment tests, patient feedback and audit.

stem: What supports continuing professional development?
options: Training updates and reflection on practice
explanation: Ongoing education and reflection help maintain competence as equipment, protocols and professional expectations change. Development is part of safe continuing practice.

stem: Which is the main artery supplying the lower limb?
explanation: The femoral artery is the major arterial supply of the lower limb. It continues from the external iliac artery beneath the inguinal ligament. The source slide says “external carotid”; this is a source typographical error. The supplied slide wording remains unchanged.

stem: Which muscles are important abductors of the hip?
explanation: Gluteus medius and minimus abduct the thigh and help stabilize the pelvis. The adductor group draws the thigh toward the midline; the other pairs act in different regions.

stem: Femoral neck fractures are clinically associated with which concern?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
explanation: The lecture identifies avascular necrosis as a key concern in femoral neck injury because blood supply to the head can be compromised. The other conditions relate to different anatomy or film processing.

stem: A Pott-type ankle fracture-dislocation may follow which mechanism described in the lecture?
explanation: Forced eversion can stress the medial ligament and injure malleolar structures. The lecture describes the resulting ankle fracture-dislocation pattern; the other movements do not act at the ankle.

stem: Which leg compartment primarily performs dorsiflexion?
explanation: The anterior compartment contains dorsiflexors and toe extensors such as tibialis anterior. The posterior group chiefly plantarflexes, while lateral fibular muscles chiefly evert.

stem: Which pair primarily plantarflexes the foot?
options: Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
explanation: Gastrocnemius and soleus are posterior leg muscles that plantarflex the ankle. Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus belong to the dorsiflexor group.

stem: Which muscles are the principal lateral-compartment evertors?
explanation: Fibularis longus and brevis occupy the lateral leg compartment and evert the foot. The hamstrings and anterior thigh muscles are not lateral leg evertors.

stem: Which muscle forms the superolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa?
explanation: Biceps femoris bounds the fossa superolaterally. Semimembranosus and semitendinosus form the superomedial boundary, and gastrocnemius contributes the inferior boundaries.

stem: How many phalanges are present in a normal foot?
explanation: The forefoot has five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges. These should not be confused with the seven tarsal bones in the hindfoot and midfoot.

stem: Which bones form the lateral longitudinal arch?
options: Talus navicular and first metatarsal only
Calcaneus cuboid and fourth and fifth metatarsals
explanation: The lateral longitudinal arch includes the calcaneus, cuboid and lateral two metatarsals. The medial arch instead includes talus, navicular and the first three metatarsals.

stem: Compared with direct-exposure film why can a screen-film system use less X-ray exposure?
options: Screens convert X-rays to light efficiently
The base becomes opaque before exposure
Screens remove all radiation before imaging
explanation: Intensifying screens convert absorbed X-ray energy into light that exposes compatible film. This amplification can reduce the X-ray exposure required compared with direct-exposure film.

stem: Which film receives a larger proportion of exposure directly from X-rays?
explanation: Direct-exposure film relies more directly on X-ray interactions. Screen film is designed mainly for the light emitted by intensifying screens.

stem: Which dental film is positioned inside the mouth?
explanation: Intraoral film is small and placed within a light-tight packet inside the mouth. Extraoral film is positioned outside, commonly in a cassette.

stem: Which listed metric film size is used for a large standard radiographic sheet?
explanation: The lecture lists 35 × 43 cm among common radiographic film sizes. The much smaller options are not that large standard sheet size.

stem: Bending film during handling is associated with which artefact?
explanation: Mechanical flexing or kinking can produce black or white crescent marks. Careful edge handling and avoiding bending reduce these pressure-related artefacts.

stem: Which roll-film size is listed for mass chest screening?
explanation: The lecture associates 100 mm roll film with mass chest screening and 105 mm with mass miniature radiography. These are historical film-based recording applications.

stem: Which photographic material is used to copy an existing radiograph?
explanation: Duplicating film reproduces existing radiographs for referral, teaching or records. It does not require the patient to undergo a new exposure merely to make that copy.

stem: Which screen material is associated with blue-sensitive film in the lecture?
explanation: Calcium tungstate emits light compatible with blue-sensitive film. The screen emission must match the film response for efficient imaging.

stem: Which film category is sensitive across much of the visible spectrum including red?
explanation: Panchromatic film responds across a broad visible spectrum. Because red light may also expose it, ordinary radiographic safelight assumptions cannot simply be applied.

stem: What is a limitation of instant photographic film described in the lecture?
options: Ability to replace all digital storage
explanation: Instant prints offer rapid output but may have limited long-term stability and higher cost per print. Their convenience should be distinguished from archival durability.

stem: Which software category includes Windows and Linux?
explanation: Windows and Linux are operating systems that manage hardware and support applications. They are distinct from clinical acquisition or image-storage applications.

stem: Which is an example of DICOM viewing software named in the lecture?
explanation: Weasis is named as a DICOM viewer for medical images. Word and Writer are document tools, while Excel is a spreadsheet.

stem: Source-to-image distance belongs to which data category?
explanation: SID is an acquisition parameter, grouped with kVp, mA, mAs and focal-spot size as technical data. It differs from demographic or interpreted diagnostic data.

stem: Which quality means information is protected against unauthorized access?
explanation: Confidentiality protects patient information from inappropriate access or disclosure. It applies to images, reports and associated records.

stem: Why should files be organized with patient identifiers examination dates and types?
options: To make every image anonymous automatically
To remove the need for backups
To support accurate retrieval and comparison
explanation: Consistent file organization helps staff locate the correct examination and compare prior studies. It does not itself create backups or anonymize data.

stem: Can digital communication occur without the public internet?
options: Yes through a private hospital network
Only if patient identifiers are removed from all records
No every transfer must be public
explanation: Digital communication is electronic information exchange and can occur on a private local network. The internet is one means of connectivity, not a requirement for every digital transfer.

stem: What is the purpose of reference-management software?
explanation: Reference managers store bibliographic details and help format citations and reference lists. They support research writing rather than image acquisition.

stem: Which resource primarily searches biomedical literature?
explanation: PubMed is listed for searching biomedical and health research. The other options are physical radiography or processing tools.

stem: Which application is specifically listed for organizing research references?
explanation: Zotero manages references and supports citation workflows. It does not operate detector readout or X-ray generation.

stem: Which organization is listed as a radiation-protection and medical-imaging information resource?
explanation: The International Atomic Energy Agency is listed as a resource for radiation protection and medical imaging. Source authority and relevance should be assessed when conducting online research.

stem: Why should students critically assess online research?
options: All websites follow the same clinical standard
Some information is false outdated or methodologically weak
Every online source is automatically peer reviewed
explanation: The lecture highlights misinformation, outdated studies and weak methods as research challenges. Students should assess evidence quality rather than assume search visibility proves reliability.

stem: Copying research text without proper acknowledgment risks what?
explanation: Using another author’s work without appropriate acknowledgment is plagiarism. Correct citation and responsible paraphrasing are essential research practices.

stem: Which is a benefit of daylight film systems?
options: Normal-light handling within a protected enclosure
Direct conversion of all film into PACS data
explanation: The light-tight loading system allows routine handling in a normally illuminated room. It still protects sensitive film and still uses conventional chemical processing.

stem: During CR readout what does a light detector convert emitted light into?
explanation: Light from the stimulated phosphor is collected and detected, producing an electrical signal for subsequent digitization. This is separate from plate erasure.

stem: Which is an advantage of CR in an existing radiography department?
options: Compatibility with many existing X-ray units
No need for any plate maintenance
explanation: CR can often be introduced using existing X-ray equipment because the cassette-based phosphor plate replaces film. Plates still need care, cleaning and erasure.

stem: Which CR plate problem can produce image artefacts?
explanation: Physical damage and contamination interfere with stored or detected image signals. Regular maintenance and careful handling reduce avoidable artefacts.

stem: Which DR conversion sequence uses a scintillator?
options: X-rays directly to printed report text
X-rays to light to electrical charge
explanation: Indirect DR first converts X-rays into light in a scintillator and then converts the light to charge in photodiodes. Direct conversion produces charge without that light stage.

stem: Which conversion material avoids the intermediate light stage in DR?
explanation: Amorphous selenium is a direct-conversion photoconductor. The other listed materials are associated with converting X-ray energy into light.

stem: After detector signals are read what forms the displayed digital radiograph?
options: Computer processing of numerical image data
Chemical fixing of a CR cassette
explanation: The detector signals are digitized and processed by a computer into a displayable image. Digital image formation does not require routine wet film processing.

stem: What does edge enhancement primarily emphasize?
explanation: Edge enhancement increases the visibility of changes between adjacent image regions. Excessive processing can mislead, so presentation should remain appropriate to the diagnostic task.

stem: What is dose creep in digital imaging?
options: Physical motion of a lead apron
Gradual unnecessary increase in exposure masked by acceptable image appearance
A fixed mandatory reduction to zero dose
explanation: Wide exposure latitude and display normalization may make overexposure less obvious than on film. Monitoring exposure indicators and appropriate technique helps control gradual increases.

stem: Why do digital imaging systems need reliable backups?
options: Image data can be lost through failures or cyberattacks
Backup files replace all confidentiality controls
explanation: Hardware, software and security failures can compromise stored images. Secure recoverable backups support continuity but must still protect confidentiality.

stem: Why is anode rotation useful in a rotating-anode tube?
options: Distribute target heat over a larger track
Remove all need for tube cooling
explanation: Rotation spreads electron bombardment across a focal track rather than concentrating heat at one stationary spot. Heat management remains essential because most electron energy becomes heat.

stem: What is an advantage of a high-frequency generator described in the lecture?
explanation: Electronic switching produces a nearly constant tube voltage and efficient consistent operation. The generator still requires power and appropriate exposure control.

stem: Which technique can reduce scatter reaching the image receptor?
explanation: An air gap allows more divergent scattered photons to miss the receptor. Collimation and appropriate grid use are other scatter-control approaches.

stem: What material forms the absorbing strips of a conventional anti-scatter grid?
explanation: Lead strips absorb off-axis radiation, while radiolucent interspaces permit aligned primary radiation to pass. Grid alignment and appropriate exposure technique remain important.

stem: What is a crossed grid?
explanation: A crossed grid combines two linear grids to reject scatter in two directions. Its geometry differs from a single linear grid.

stem: Mammography equipment is specialized for imaging which anatomy?
explanation: Mammography is a dedicated breast X-ray imaging system used for detection and evaluation of breast disease. It is not a general-purpose extremity-only system.

stem: Before processing patient films after startup what condition should be reached?
explanation: The processor needs time to reach a stable operating condition before patient films are introduced. Tank levels, water supply and drain status also require checks.

stem: Damp film at processor exit should prompt which check?
explanation: Inadequate drying heat, exhausted fixer or hardener issues can contribute to wet film. Troubleshooting should check the relevant processor systems rather than unrelated workstation settings.

stem: Why should actual developer temperature be measured independently?
explanation: An independent check can reveal an inaccurate temperature display or control problem. Temperature verification complements control-film measurements.

stem: How can replenishment delivery be checked?
options: Measure the volume pumped for a known film workload
Count the letters in a report
explanation: Comparing actual delivered volume with the specified replenishment setting checks pump performance. The lecture includes this as a weekly QA activity.

stem: The brachial plexus commonly arises from which spinal nerve roots?
explanation: The lecture identifies ventral rami C5 through T1 as the roots of the brachial plexus. This plexus supplies the upper limb.

stem: Which bone is described as the first to begin ossification?
explanation: The lecture notes that clavicular ossification begins early in intrauterine life. This feature distinguishes it from the other bones listed.

stem: The humeral capitulum articulates with which structure?
explanation: The distal humeral capitulum lies laterally and articulates with the radial head. The trochlea lies medially and articulates with the ulna.

stem: The humeral trochlea articulates with which forearm bone?
explanation: The medial pulley-shaped trochlea forms the humeroulnar articulation. The lateral capitulum receives the radial head.

stem: Which needs are included in holistic patient care in the lecture?
explanation: Patient care addresses the person’s physical, emotional and social needs. Technical image quality is essential but is only one part of the overall care experience.

stem: What is an essential professional boundary for a technician?
options: Work within the authorized scope of practice
explanation: Professional practice requires understanding duties, competence and authorized scope. Team members should seek appropriate assistance for tasks outside that scope.

stem: Which is an appropriate equipment-cleaning approach?
options: Clean only when an infection is confirmed
Use approved disinfectant on relevant surfaces
explanation: Tables, cassettes and equipment contact surfaces require appropriate cleaning with approved agents. Standard precautions do not depend on knowing a patient’s infection status.

stem: Which landmark separates the two buttocks?
explanation: The intergluteal cleft separates the buttocks. The gluteal fold instead marks the inferior boundary of the gluteal region.

explanation: The AP knee instructions call for slight joint flexion. This is a positioning detail distinct from the already tested patellar alignment and centring point.
sourceExcerpt: Place the affected knee on the film and flex the joint slightly
sourceEvidence:

KNEE
AP Projection for  Knee
Lie the patient on the X-ray couch on the affected side with legs extended and unaffected leg abducted
Place the affected knee on the film and flex the joint slightly
Ensure that the patella is central over the femur
Immobilize the leg
Collimate beam and apply protection
Place anatomical marker (R or L)
Cassette size  : 12x10inch or 10x8inch
DCR:: Vertical
CP: 2.5cm below the apex of the patella
Exposure factors
Kvp: 55-75, mAs: 5-10 and FFD: 100cm

stem: Which centring point is stated for the lateral knee projection in the supplied lecture?
options: Midline skin crease behind the knee
Middle of the superior border of the medial tibial condyle
explanation: The lateral-knee section gives the middle of the superior border of the medial tibial condyle as its centring point. The other options belong to separate projections in the same deck.
sourceExcerpt: CP: Middle of the superior border of the medial tibia condyle
sourceEvidence:
Lateral projection for Knee
Lie the patient on the X-ray couch on the affected side with the  knee flexed at 45 or 90 degrees
Rest the unaffected leg in a comfortable position in front of  the affected leg.
Place the knee in the true lateral position
Immobilize the leg and ankle with sandbag.
Collimate beam and apply protection
Place anatomical marker (R or L)
DCR:: Vertical or Horizontal (if cassette is placed at the lateral part of the leg in case of)
CP: Middle of the superior border of the medial tibia condyle
PA for Patella
Patient lie prone on the table with knee slightly flexed
Foam pads are placed under the ankle and thigh for support
The limb is rotated to centralize the patella
The centre of the cassette is the level of the crease of the knee
Immobile the leg
Place anatomical marker
Collimate
DCR: Vertical
CP: In the midline to the skin crease behind the knee
